name: Victor Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I supervise three line crews on the edge of the city, where the new housing estates are going up, so it's mostly new connections: new poles, new underground cable to whole streets, chargers for electric cars, solar panels feeding back into the grid. I start at six-thirty with a coffee and the AI assistant on my laptop, which drafts the job packs from the drawings, checks the materials list and flags anything that clashes with the gas or water lines. Then I'm out visiting the crews, flying a drone over a new route, sorting out a builder who's dug where he shouldn't. Some days I still get up a pole when a crew's short, because I miss it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy building something that wasn't there. A field becomes a street and I'm the guy who made the lights come on. What wears me out is builders who don't read the plans, and meetings that could have been an email. My wife Clara jokes that I've got more apps than friends, which isn't quite true, but close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool, not a miracle. At work I'd keep showing people the useful bits. Online I'd probably post something about how the people who said it would change everything and the people who said it was useless were both wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I already get an hour a day back from the job packs, so I'd keep that. Honestly, I'd be a little bored, like buying a sports car and finding out the speed limit is thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using what works and keep my retirement at sixty-two. I'd probably shift a bit of the money I've got in technology shares into something steadier, since the big promise didn't come through. Otherwise the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a touch disappointed. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What would you miss if it never got better than now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The idea of it getting better, I suppose. I was hoping it would start reading the drone footage and telling me which poles are rotten, so my lads don't have to tap every one with a hammer. In this picture, we keep tapping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your money or plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just the shares. I've got a fair bit in a fund that tracks robotics and AI companies, maybe fifteen percent of our savings. If the hype died, I'd move most of that into something boring before everybody else did.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a good tool, not a miracle, and post that both the hype merchants and the doubters were wrong. At work he'd keep showing people the useful bits.
S0.think: He thinks it's fine for him since he already gets an hour a day back, but he'd be a little bored. It would feel like a fast car stuck at a low speed limit.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI tools that work and keeps his retirement date at sixty-two. Moves most of the roughly fifteen percent of savings he holds in a robotics and AI fund into steadier investments.
S0.feel: Calm, a touch disappointed, nothing to lose sleep over.
S0.quote: Honestly, I'd be a little bored, like buying a sports car and finding out the speed limit is thirty.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is an early adopter who uses AI daily for job packs and drones and enjoys new tools for their own sake. He already holds a robotics fund, so even the plateau triggers a money move. His centre outlook shows in his dismissal of both extremes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the sensible version: change, but with time to adjust. At work I'd say let's be the depot that gets it right first. Online I'd share what's working for us, without the sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good. I'm the guy who already likes this stuff, so I'd be useful. In this picture I'm the one they send to the meetings, and for once I wouldn't mind going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the trials of any new robots and sensors on our estates, starting next spring. I'd put a bit more into the robotics fund. I'd also set up short sessions for the crews, Friday afternoons, half an hour each, showing them the tools I already use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Excited, with a bit of worry for some of the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crews would struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of my older lineworkers, Ray and Mick. Both brilliant on the pole, but they won't touch a tablet unless you threaten them. I'd want to keep them on the hands-on work and let the younger ones take the screens, so nobody feels useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be supervising during the change. What would you do differently from other supervisors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the crews try the tools before management chose them. If the lads who use it every day say it's rubbish, it's rubbish. I've seen too many systems bought because they looked good in a meeting.

S1.say: He'd call this the sensible version and want his depot to be the first to get it right. Online he'd share what's working without a sales pitch.
S1.think: He thinks it's good for him because he already likes the technology and would be useful. For once he wouldn't mind being sent to the meetings.
S1.do: Asks to lead trials of new robots and sensors on the estates from next spring and adds to his robotics fund. Runs short Friday training sessions for his crews and lets them try tools before management chooses.
S1.feel: Pretty good, excited with a bit of worry for some of the older crew members.
S1.quote: In this picture I'm the one they send to the meetings, and for once I wouldn't mind going.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as his moment and immediately thinks about how to bring his crews along, including two older men he'd keep on hands-on work. He wants the people who use the tools to choose them. His money move is to add to his robotics fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for most people, and companies and the government need to stop pretending it's not happening. At work I'd say let's be useful, help set up the machines properly, because a badly installed robot on a live line is a disaster. Online I'd probably share practical stuff, not opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be okay. I'm adaptable, I know the systems, and I've got savings and shares. The machines will need someone to tell them where the gas main is, and that's still going to be me for a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd offer to lead the rollout at the depot, and I'd talk to the robot suppliers about consulting work on line installations, two days a month. I'd sit down with Clara and work out what we'd do if her job and our son's gym got hit, and I'd keep some cash ready to help him. I'd hold the shares, not sell in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, but for everyone around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your robotics fund would probably jump in this picture. How do you feel about making money from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange, to be honest. I'd be one of the winners while my lads lose their jobs. I'd probably use some of it to help the people around me, my son, maybe one of the crew who's in trouble. It wouldn't feel right otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clara's a school business manager, and a lot of what she does is paperwork, so she'd be hit. My son Lukas runs a gym, and if people lose jobs, gym memberships are the first thing to go. My daughter Hanna's training as a nurse, so maybe she's safer, but who knows. I'd be fine, and everyone I love would be wobbling.

S2.say: He'd say it's too fast for most people and companies and government must stop pretending. At work he'd urge everyone to help install the machines properly, since a badly installed robot on a live line is a disaster.
S2.think: He thinks he'd be okay with his skills, savings and shares, and still needed for a while to guide the machines. He knows his position is unusually secure.
S2.do: Offers to lead the depot rollout and seeks two days a month of consulting with robot suppliers. Plans with his wife for her job and their son's gym being hit, keeps cash ready to help his son, and holds his shares rather than panic-selling.
S2.feel: Uneasy, less for himself than for everyone around him.
S2.quote: I'd be fine, and everyone I love would be wobbling.
S2.fieldNote: He's honest that he'd be a winner while his crew lose out, and that makes him uncomfortable. His instinct is to use the gains to help family and colleagues. His wife's paperwork-heavy job and his son's gym are where his worry sits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, there's time, so get on with it. At work I'd say every crew should have someone trained on the robots by 2029. I'd write a few practical posts about what we've learned on the trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's almost ideal. I'd have time to build up the consulting side and leave the company on my own terms. Five years is enough to turn what I know about poles and cables into a second career that doesn't need my knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the depot's robot trials, get some kind of certificate in robot installation by 2028, and start the consulting work properly. I'd move some of the shares into property, maybe a small rental, so we're not all in one basket. Clara and I would plan for her to retrain if she wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite energised. It feels like something to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change your plans for retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I might stay to sixty-three and do consulting on the side, or retire at sixty-two and consult full-time for a couple of years. Either way, I'd want to be inside it, not watching from the sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ray and Mick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get to sixty-two and take their pensions, and I'd try to make sure they're doing the hands-on jobs until then. They don't need to learn robotics at sixty. They need someone to protect them for a few years, and that's my job as supervisor.

S3.say: He'd say it's coming and there's time, so get on with it, with every crew having someone trained on robots by 2029. He'd write practical posts about the trials.
S3.think: He thinks five years is almost ideal: enough to turn his knowledge of poles and cables into a second career that doesn't need his knees.
S3.do: Leads depot robot trials, earns a robot installation certificate by 2028 and builds up consulting work. Moves some shares into a small rental property and plans with his wife for her to retrain if she wants.
S3.feel: Calm and energised, with something to plan for.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to turn what I know about poles and cables into a second career that doesn't need my knees.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year picture is close to his ideal. He'd use the time to build a second career and diversify his money. His protective attitude to his two older linemen shows a supervisor who thinks about people, not just machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. At work I'd say start the training now, not in year eight. I'd post about practical plans, not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be retired before it fully lands, but I'd probably still be doing a bit of consulting. The danger with ten years is that everyone does nothing for nine of them. I'd want to be the annoying one who starts early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools every day, keep the robotics fund, retire at sixty-two, and build up some consulting on the side. I'd help Lukas think about what his gym looks like in a world where people have more free time, which might actually be good for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave it too late with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For other people, yes. For me, no, I'm always early on these things. My worry is the company will wait till year nine and then panic-buy whatever robot the salesman shows them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to get right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start small, test properly in real weather, and keep the people who know the network involved. And don't let anyone retire without writing down what they know first. That's the most valuable thing we've got.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a gift and urge his depot to start training now, not in year eight. He'd post practical plans rather than end-of-the-world talk.
S4.think: He thinks he'd be retired before it fully lands but still consulting. His worry is everyone doing nothing for nine of the ten years.
S4.do: Keeps using AI daily, holds the robotics fund, retires at sixty-two and builds consulting work on the side. Helps his son think about how his gym might do well in a world with more free time.
S4.quote: My worry is the company will wait till year nine and then panic-buy whatever robot the salesman shows them.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he's relaxed about himself but worried about institutional delay and panic-buying. He wants knowledge written down before people retire. He even sees a possible upside for his son's gym, which says a lot about his optimistic streak.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be fine and everyone around me wouldn't be. What would help is the government and companies sitting down together early, quick retraining that's actually about real jobs, and some kind of income support for people while they work out their next move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what goes wrong. Robots on live lines will have accidents, and when they do, it'll be someone like me who has to go and sort it out. I hope they keep enough people with real skills around for that.

headlineQuote: The danger with ten years is that everyone does nothing for nine of them.
portrait: Victor Bauer is a 58-year-old supervisor of three line crews on the fast-growing edge of a city, connecting new housing estates, chargers and solar panels. He uses AI every day for job packs and flies drones, and he holds a fair amount of savings in a robotics fund. He's calm or even excited in the plateau and steady change pictures, eager to lead trials and bring his crews along. In the two-year AGI picture he's uneasy because he'd do well while his wife, son and crews struggle, and with five or ten years he'd build a consulting career and push his company to start early.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries him most, because he'd be fine and everyone around him wouldn't be.
whatWouldHelp: Government and companies planning together early, quick retraining for real jobs, and income support while people work out their next move.
